summary: Lets two communicating SIP proxies reuse one congestion-controlled connection for requests in both directions. Because of this aliasing, both sides must authenticate with X.509 certificates over TLS, which is covered for TCP and SCTP. It also gives guidance on virtual servers and DNS SRV. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of two phone lines between offices, they use one line for talking both ways, after each side proves who they are.

questions: reusing tls connections between sip proxies
what is the sip alias parameter
how does sip tls connection reuse work
sip persistent connection vs connection reuse
subtitle: How two SIP peers can reuse one authenticated TLS connection to send requests in both directions.

tldr.problem: SIP entities usually open a connection from an ephemeral port, so requests going the other way tend to need a second connection. For TLS that means extra handshakes, CPU load and delay.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds an alias parameter to its topmost Via header. If the server authenticates the client's X.509 certificate and agrees, both sides record the connection in an alias table and reuse it, but only for destinations whose URI matches an identity in the cached certificate.
tldr.outcome: Fewer connections and less setup delay, with protection against connection hijacking. It is limited to TLS, and the server may ignore the request.

today: RFC 5923 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on RFC 3261, RFC 3263 and RFC 5922.

sections.title: Two Connections Where One Would Do
sections.content:
When SIP entities use a connection-oriented transport such as TCP or SCTP, they typically open connections from an ephemeral port. In the RFC's example, A listens on port 5061 (the default for SIP over TLS over TCP) but connects to B from ephemeral port 49160.

SIP's persistent connection lets responses and later requests from the originator reuse that connection. But new requests in the backwards direction, from B to A, are unlikely to reuse it. So a pair of entities often ends up with one connection for each direction.

With TLS, each end can be authenticated when the connection is set up, so the connection can safely be reused backwards. The RFC calls this connection reuse or aliasing. It is different from a persistent connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Two offices each call the other on their own phone line. This says: they could just share one line, as long as each knows who is on the other end.

sections.title: Where It Applies and Why Bother
sections.content:
The mechanism is for two adjacent SIP entities that do not care which side opens the connection. Entities that can only connect in one direction, perhaps because of NAT and firewalls, use the outbound mechanism of RFC 5626 instead. The RFC says it is good practice to reuse only connections whose sender can be verified, so TLS connections formed with X.509 certificates qualify.

The benefit is performance. Each new TLS connection needs a TCP three-way handshake, several round trips for TLS, costly asymmetric cryptography and certificate verification, which can saturate a server's CPU. In a call where proxies use Record-Route, Proxy B would open a new connection just to send a BYE. A new connection for a re-INVITE could delay it by several round trips, enough for a person to notice.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a new line takes a lot of work, like checking ID at the door every time. Reusing the line saves that work and waiting.

sections.title: How the Alias Works
sections.content:
Proxy P1 starts by adding an alias parameter to the Via header it inserts, for example Via: SIP/2.0/TLS p1.example.com;branch=z9hG4bKa7c8dze;alias. The sent-by value and transport become its advertised address. P1 resolves P2 with RFC 3263, opens the connection, authenticates P2's certificate, and records P2 in its alias table: IP address, port, transport, the identities from the certificate, and the socket descriptor.

P1 reuses the connection later only if the resolved address is in the table and the URI used for resolution matches one of the cached identities.

When P2 sees the alias parameter, it authenticates P1, and if that succeeds it builds its own table row. The address comes from the source address (the received parameter), the port from the Via header or 5061 if absent, and the identities from the client certificate. P2 then reuses the connection under the same two conditions. The RFC says it does not standardize the alias table itself, which is only a teaching aid.
sections.plainLanguage: P1 says, "you can call me back on this line." P2 checks P1's ID, writes down who is on the line, and uses it only for calls to that same person.

sections.title: Client and Server Rules
sections.content:
Clients SHOULD keep connections up as long as needed and SHOULD NOT drop them after a transaction or dialog ends. A client that sends the alias parameter MUST accept requests over that connection, in addition to its default listening port, and SHOULD reuse the connection for later requests to the same resolved address. It gets no confirmation that the server created an alias, so it MUST NOT assume one and MUST keep receiving on its default port. It MUST authenticate the connection before forming an alias.

The server decides whether to honor the alias. If it does not, it MUST handle the request as though the parameter were absent, so clients can include it without fear of rejection. If the server uses the alias, it MUST authenticate first and cache the identities from the certificate's subjectAlternativeName extension. If the connection is gone when it is needed, either side MUST open a new one and update the table.

If a connection closed before a CANCEL or an ACK for a non-2xx response, the client SHOULD open a new one. Before closing a TLS connection, the initiator MUST wait for outstanding transactions or abandon them, and the receiver of the closure alert MUST NOT start new transactions.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking to share the line is always polite and safe. The other side can say no by simply not using it, and if the line drops, they just call again.

sections.title: Security and Virtual Servers
sections.content:
Unauthenticated reuse would invite abuse and hijacking. The RFC's example is a program run by a malicious user of a multiuser system that tries to hijack SIP requests meant for a large relay proxy's well-known port. The client authenticates the server as described in RFC 5922. A TLS server MUST ask for a client certificate. If the client has none, the server MUST proceed as if alias were absent and MUST NOT update its alias table.

With name-based virtual servers, one proxy hosts many domains on one address and port. A connection opened for one domain must not be reused for another. That is why the table keeps the identity column. Virtual servers MUST do connection reuse only over TLS, because a plain TCP or SCTP connection has no identity tied to it. In the example, P2 cannot reuse its cached connection to 192.0.2.1 for example.net, because the cached identity is example.com, so it opens a second connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing a line is only safe if you know who is on it. If one building houses two companies, you do not use one company's line to call the other.

sections.title: Load Balancing with DNS SRV
sections.content:
Connection reuse interacts with DNS SRV load balancing. If a proxy spreads traffic over servers S1, S2 and S3, it will over time keep a distinct aliased connection to each of them. After that, subsequent traffic is still load balanced across the three downstream servers in the normal manner.

For IANA, the RFC registers the alias Via header field parameter in the Header Field Parameters and Parameter Values sub-registry created by RFC 3968. Its formal syntax is via-params =/ via-alias with via-alias = "alias".
sections.plainLanguage: Even with one shared line to each of three shops, you still pick which shop to call as before.
